l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The perfect man is distinguished not by outward bodily difference but by seeing what is not to be seen and by spiritual freedom. His doctrine responds like a shadow to form or an echo to sound, guiding humanity without plans or entanglement.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Sage looks up to God, perfects virtue, follows TAO, identifies with charity, extends duty, responds to ceremony, undertakes affairs, applies law, relies on fellow-men, and accommodates himself to matter. His action is ultimately inaction rather than premeditated interference.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: This unit concerns the universe, TAO, and the relation of God, virtue, inaction, and all things. It describes how the empire was once governed through inaction and natural order, and defines the true Sage as one who embodies complete virtue and follows TAO. It contrasts spiritual realization through Nothing with the limitations of knowledge, sight, speech, intelligence, wealth, and worldly power. It also recounts teachings and encounters involving Lao Tzŭ, Yao, and others, explaining how cultivation of nature leads back to virtue and the unconditioned.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: The universe is vast, regular in its phenomena, uniform in the laws governing its contents, and dominated by sovereignty. It is covered and supported by TAO, and the true Sage becomes united with it by following the natural order.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: TAO informs and governs all things, spreads throughout creation, and connects virtue, duty, and natural conditions. It is the source through which form, life, intelligence, and the complete virtue of the Sage are realized.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: God is associated with sovereignty that begins in virtue and is called divine. The true Sage may pass into the kingdom of God, and unconsciousness of objective existences and of God is described as combining the human and divine.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Virtue is the connecting link between God and man and is the means by which things are what they are. By cultivating nature, beings return to virtue, and by perfecting virtue they become unconditioned and aligned with the beginning of all things.

l: Inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Inaction governed the empire of old, allowing natural conditions to prevail over artificial arrangements. Through inaction, the sovereign avoided cruel mandates, people fulfilled their roles, officials governed appropriately, and all things proceeded on their course.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: The empire was once described as being under the sovereignty of inaction and TAO, with clear duties, proper officials, and harmony among all things. When rulers relied on reward and punishment instead of virtue, the decline of virtue and the reign of force began.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: The true Sage follows TAO, cultivates virtue in retirement when necessary, and remains in harmony with all things. He does not strive for wealth, fame, success, or personal glory, and he can perceive light in darkness and harmony in stillness.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Man is controlled by outward circumstances and applies in-born skill to civilized life, but his senses and intelligence can obscure his spiritual nature. Man advances toward the divine by becoming unconscious of objective existences and cultivating his own nature.

l: all things, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: All things exist under their own natural conditions and respond to proper influences in accordance with TAO. They arise through ONE, receive their virtue, acquire form and nature, and may be brought back toward their original unconditioned state.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Lao Tzŭ is associated with the Record and with teachings about TAO, inaction, and the natural order. He tells Confucius that rigid rules and distinctions are merely handicraft skill and that true understanding cannot be fully expressed in words.

l: Nothing, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Nothing successfully recovers the Yellow Emperor's lost magic pearl after Intelligence, Sight, and Speech fail. The text teaches that true spirituality is found in a state of negation rather than through knowledge, sight, or speech.

l: Yao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Yao is portrayed as an emperor who consults Hsü Yu about suitable rulers and later visits Hua, where he rejects wishes for long life, wealth, and many sons. He is also associated with handing the empire to Shun.

l: the natural, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XII.
s: Nature is the original condition that should prevail over artificial arrangements. By cultivating nature, one is carried back to virtue and ultimately becomes unconditioned, in accordance with the eternal fitness of things.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Chiang Lü Mien asks Chi Ch'ê about governing, and Chi Ch'ê explains that the Sage influences people according to their natural dispositions. Tzŭ Kung meets an old gardener who rejects a well-sweep as contrary to purity and Tao, then reports the encounter to Confucius. Chun Mang describes the government of the Sage, the man of perfect virtue, and the divine man to Yüan Fêng. Mên Wu Kuei and Ch'ih Chang Man Chi discuss the Great Yü, the Golden Age, the errors of the world, and the loss of original nature through sensory and social distractions.

l: Chiang Lü Mien, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Chiang Lü Mien tells Chi Ch'ê that he instructed the Prince of Lu to be decorous and thrifty, advance the public-spirited and loyal, and avoid partialities. He admits uncertainty about his doctrine and asks Chi Ch'ê for instruction.

l: Chi Ch'ê, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Chi Ch'ê criticizes Chiang Lü Mien's advice as ineffective and compares it to a mantis trying to stop a carriage. He explains that the government of the perfect Sage works by influencing people according to their natural dispositions, so that they become virtuous without being conscious of the influence.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Tao is presented as incompatible with cunning implements, cunning dealings, restless spirits, and attachment to success, profit, and skill. The divine man is described as being at one with God and man and as bringing all things back to their original state.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The Sage governs by allowing officials to perform their functions, employing ability, hearing the people's voice, and keeping the empire at peace. The Sage's government influences people naturally, while the Sage blushes when a filial son must administer medicine to a sick father.

l: Tzŭ Kung, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Tzŭ Kung offers an old gardener a well-sweep, but is rebuked for promoting cunning and self-display. He later tells Confucius about the encounter and reflects that the gardener's way differs from the practical doctrines he had attributed to Confucius.

l: old gardener, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The old gardener irrigates his garden by carrying water in a pitcher and refuses Tzŭ Kung's well-sweep because he believes cunning implements produce cunning dealings and restless spirits unfit for Tao. He rebukes Tzŭ Kung for seeking reputation and trying to govern others without governing himself.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Confucius tells Tzŭ Kung that the gardener understands only the internal and not the external, and that there is nothing extraordinary in returning to original integrity through clarity and inaction. He also says that the science of the ante-mundane is not worth knowing to them.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Perfect virtue is associated with governing by natural influence and with a person who has no thought in repose, no anxiety in action, and no attachment to distinctions of right and wrong or good and bad. Such a person has wealth and food without knowing their source and is followed by people who cling to him like lost children.

l: government of the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The government of the Sage confines officials to their functions, secures employment for ability, hears the people's voice, and lets men own their words and deeds. It brings peace through responsive and natural action rather than overt coercion.

l: Chun Mang, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Chun Mang travels eastward to the ocean and tells Yüan Fêng how the Sage governs. He also describes the man of perfect virtue and the divine man.

l: Yüan Fêng, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Yüan Fêng meets Chun Mang on the shore of the eastern sea and questions him about the ocean, the Sage, the man of perfect virtue, and the divine man.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The divine man rides upon the glory of the sky until his form cannot be discerned, fulfilling his destiny and acting according to his nature. He is at one with God and man, for whom affairs cease to exist and all things return to their original state.

l: Great Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The Great Yü is discussed as a ruler who dealt with disorder, though Ch'ih Chang Man Chi says that if the empire had already been properly governed, there would have been nothing for him to do. He is compared to ointment applied to a sore.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: The empire is described as peaceful under the Sage when officials perform their functions, ability is employed, and the people's voice is heard. In the Golden Age, people acted freely and virtuously without conscious duties or conventions, leaving no trace in history.

l: Golden Age, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: During the Golden Age, rulers served as mere beacons and people lived freely like wild deer. People were upright, loving, truthful, honest, and unconstrained without consciously recognizing duty, charity, loyalty, good faith, or obligation.

l: original nature, Chuang Tzŭ, Chiang Lü Mien went to see Chi Ch'ê,
s: Original nature is lost when the five colours, sounds, scents, tastes, and likes and dislikes overwhelm the senses and understanding. The text says that both highly honoured objects and despised conditions can involve destruction of original nature.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The chapter teaches that TAO operates ceaselessly through repose, stillness, and inaction, from which movement, order, and accomplishment arise. It explains that the Sage and wise ruler should model themselves on GOD, cultivating essentials rather than accidental forms such as ceremonies, laws, rewards, and punishments. Yao, Shun, Confucius, Lao Tzŭ, Shih Ch'êng Ch'i, Duke Huan, and a wheelwright illustrate the limits of human action, moral doctrines, written words, and knowledge that cannot be conveyed. The chapter concludes that TAO is vast, unconditioned, and not fully expressible through forms, names, books, or speech.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: TAO operates ceaselessly and produces all things. It is associated with repose, stillness, inaction, and the proper sequence from the unconditioned to the conditioned. It cannot be fully conveyed through books, words, forms, or names.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: GOD operates ceaselessly and is associated with the universe’s spontaneous production and order. The happiness of GOD consists in supporting and shaping all things without claiming cruelty, charity, age, or skill.

l: repose, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Repose is the mental equilibrium of the Sage and is not ordinary inactivity. It gives rise to movement, attainment, inaction, potential action, happiness, and long life.

l: TAO of inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Inaction enables all things to be accomplished and gives the ruler energy to spare in administering the empire. It produces action spontaneously and unconsciously when inner repose has been achieved.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The universe is the model upon which the wise ruler’s virtue is formed. It is described as the vehicle upon which the ruler travels, with all creation as his team.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The empire rallies around the sovereign whose TAO operates ceaselessly. It is administered through the ruler’s inaction and the ruled’s action, and it becomes united when the ruler acts in accord with TAO.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Sage operates ceaselessly through repose, and his mind becomes a mirror of the universe. He cultivates essentials, remains free from care, and does not join struggles for power.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Virtue is associated with spontaneous action and with the proper ordering of essentials and accidentals. The wise ruler’s virtue is modeled upon the universe, guided by TAO, and expressed through inaction.

l: action, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Action arises from movement and follows established inner repose. The ruled must practise action to subserve the interests of the empire, while rulers who rely on action find their energy inadequate.

l: Yao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Yao succeeds as a ruler through understanding repose, tranquillity, stillness, and inaction. He tells Shun that he protects the defenceless, poor, dying, orphaned, and widowed, but Shun says this is good rather than great.

l: Shun, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Shun serves as Yao’s minister and teaches him to be passive like the virtue of GOD. He says that heaven, the sun, moon, seasons, day, night, clouds, and rain operate without deliberate striving.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Chuang Tzŭ describes the happiness of GOD as destroying, benefiting, supporting, and shaping all things without claiming cruelty, charity, age, or skill.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Confucius travels west to place his works in the Imperial library of the House of Chou. He defends charity and duty to one's neighbour as rooted in man's original nature, but Lao Tzŭ rejects his account as confusing the mind of man.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Lao Tzŭ rejects Confucius’s doctrines of charity and duty to one's neighbour and urges following TAO and the regularity of the universe. He accepts classifications that accord with truth and teaches that TAO, virtue, charity, duty, ceremonies, music, books, and words must not be confused with essentials.

l: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i first accuses Lao Tzŭ of lacking charity and being stingy, then apologizes when Lao Tzŭ remains silent. Lao Tzŭ criticizes his self-satisfied, hasty, and overconfident manner, saying such men are not trusted.

l: Duke Huan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Duke Huan studies the words of the Sages. When a wheelwright calls those words the dregs of the ancients, the Duke threatens him and demands an explanation.

l: Heaven, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Heaven has no parturitions, yet all things are evolved. It is associated with ceaseless revolution, spiritual honour, and the virtue that the wise ruler should emulate.

l: Earth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Earth knows no increment, yet all things are nourished. It is associated with stillness, lowliness in spiritual rank, and the virtue that the wise ruler should emulate.

l: the ruled, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The ruled must practise action in order to subserve the interests of the empire. If both rulers and ruled practise inaction, the ruled will equal the rulers rather than remain their subjects.

l: the ancients, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The ancients cultivated accidentals but did not allow them to precede essentials. Their words and forms may preserve traces of TAO, but the wheelwright says the words of dead Sages are only their dregs.

l: charity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Charity is presented by Confucius as rejoicing in all things and universal love without self. Lao Tzŭ treats it as an accidental of the spiritual and questions whether universal love and elimination of self contradict themselves.

l: duty to one's neighbour, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Duty to one's neighbour is presented by Confucius as part of man's original nature and as necessary to make the superior man effective. Lao Tzŭ treats it as an accidental of the spiritual rather than an essential.

l: government, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Government is perfected by following the sequence from TAO and GOD through charity, public functions, forms, capacities, distinctions, and punishments. Ceremonies and laws are described as the lowest form of government and as instruments used by the ruled in service of rulers.

l: forms and names, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Forms and names arise after earlier stages in the understanding of TAO. To rise directly to them is to ignore their source, and using them without understanding the great principle gives only the instrumental part of government.

l: rewards and punishments, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Rewards and punishments are the lowest form of education. They should be considered only after the earlier phases of TAO, forms, names, capabilities, and distinctions have been understood.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The perfect man places himself outside the universe and beyond all creation, where his soul is free from care. He apprehends TAO, remains in accord with virtue, and treats charity, duty, ceremonies, and music as adventitious.

l: the wheelwright, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The wheelwright interrupts Duke Huan’s reading and argues that the words of dead Sages are only their dregs. He explains through wheel-making that a mysterious coordination of mind and hand cannot be taught through words, even to his son.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: This unit concerns TAO, virtue, charity, duty to one's neighbour, and the encounters among Chuang Tzŭ, Confucius, and Lao Tzŭ. Chuang Tzŭ teaches that perfect charity does not admit of love for the individual and that TAO does not admit of sub-division. Lao Tzŭ criticizes Confucius's reliance on charity, duty to one's neighbour, and the ancient canons, while Confucius eventually recognizes Lao Tzŭ's wisdom and later attains TAO. The Yin and Yang principles appear as part of the cosmic order and as a harmony expressed in perfect music.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches Tang that tigers and wolves possess charity through the natural love between parents and offspring. He explains that perfect charity does not admit of love for the individual and that TAO does not admit of sub-division.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Confucius is criticized for trying to apply ancient customs and teachings without adapting them to changing circumstances. After speaking with Lao Tzŭ, he recognizes Lao Tzŭ as a Dragon whom he could not admonish, and he later attains TAO.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Lao Tzŭ tells Confucius that TAO cannot be presented, imparted, or given unless there is suitable inner endowment and outward correctness. He criticizes charity, duty to one's neighbour, the Six Canons, and the administrations of ancient rulers as inadequate or harmful when treated as fixed doctrines.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: TAO is described as indivisible and impossible to give or receive through external instruction alone. It operates through suitable inner endowment and outward correctness, and once attained there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

l: charity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Chuang Tzŭ distinguishes ordinary charity, including the natural love between parents and offspring, from perfect charity, which does not admit of love for the individual. Lao Tzŭ later calls talk of charity a distraction from the world's original simplicity.

l: duty to one's neighbour, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Duty to one's neighbour is described as one of the studied efforts intended to aid the development of virtue. Lao Tzŭ says it is like a caravanserai where one may stop briefly on the way to transcendental space, but not remain for long.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Virtue is said to establish itself naturally, without undue effort. True virtue does nothing yet surpasses Yao and Shun, and its influence may extend through ten thousand generations without being recognized.

l: Confucius's visit to Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: During Confucius's visit to Lao Tzŭ, Lao Tzŭ questions his search for TAO and explains why TAO cannot simply be transmitted. After the visit, Confucius remains silent for three days and says he saw a Dragon whose presence left him unable to admonish him.

l: Confucius's attainment of TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: After speaking with Lao Tzŭ about the Six Canons, Confucius stays at home for three months. He then returns and says that he has attained, recognizing that natural developments proceed according to fixed laws and that one who is not enlightened cannot enlighten others.

l: Positive and Negative principles, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Yin and Yang principles are listed among the Six Influences and are associated with the ordering of the world. In the Yellow Emperor's account of perfect music, their harmony produces changing, interwoven sounds that bring creation into accord.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: The chapter concerns self-conceit, the Sage, and the way of TAO through passivity, repose, and freedom from worldly attachment. It rejects social withdrawal, moral preaching, government, bodily regimens, and other efforts as incomplete substitutes for spiritual calm. The Sage is described as passive, untroubled by happiness or misfortune, and guided by the laws of God. The chapter concludes that preserving pure spirituality enables unity with God and re-absorption into the eternity from which the soul came.

l: self-conceit, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: Self-conceit is described as personal over-estimation that leads people to withdraw from society, distinguish themselves from others, indulge in tall talk, and abuse others.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Sage possesses self-esteem without self-conceit, retirement without solitude, and health without hygiene. The Sage is passive and at repose, makes no plans, is unaffected by honour or blame, and floats through life to rest in death.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: TAO is characterized by tranquillity, stillness, the unconditioned, and inaction. Its pure and simple way consists in preserving spirituality and allowing it to operate freely in relationship with God.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: God determines the Sage's birth and the modification of existence that is death. The Sage shares the passivity of the Yin in repose and the energy of the Yang in action, while pure spirituality is nourished according to TAO and brought into relationship with God.

l: spirituality, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: Spirituality is described as extending everywhere, reaching heaven and embracing earth, though its form cannot be portrayed. Preserving it without loss makes a person one with spirituality and allows it to operate freely.

l: soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: The soul is valued by Sages above money, fame, and resolution. It returns after its brief career on earth to the eternity from which it came.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: Virtue is complete when the Sage remains passive and at repose, free from sorrow, anxiety, and foul influences. Perfect virtue is also associated with a heart unconscious of sorrow and happiness.

l: passivity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: Passivity makes the Sage negative in relation to activity and places the Sage in repose. It prevents sorrow and anxiety from entering and allows virtue to become complete and spirituality to remain unimpaired.

l: repose, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XV.
s: Repose accompanies passivity and excludes sorrow, anxiety, and foul influences. In repose, the Sage shares the passivity of the Yin and remains free from plans and worldly disturbance.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The chapter concerns TAO, Virtue, and the decline of human harmony from primeval unity into coercion, government, intellectualism, and confusion. Primeval man lived in tranquillity, with knowledge arising from repose and all things existing as one without being deliberately made so. As Virtue declined, rulers introduced systems, moral reform, art, learning, and government, causing natural instinct and original integrity to be lost. The Sages and retired scholars preserved themselves by avoiding worldly display, remaining within their natural spheres, and seeking complete happiness rather than office.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: TAO is order, but it cannot be attained through mundane arts or worldly study. The world and TAO mutually destroy each other, and TAO cannot elevate the world.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Virtue is harmony and was once all-embracing, giving rise to charity. As Virtue declined, coercion, government, goodness, art, and learning led man away from TAO and natural instinct.

l: the world, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The world destroys TAO, while TAO destroys the world, so neither can elevate the other. The world is described as becoming confused when art and learning overwhelm original constitution and mind.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The empire was once governed in natural unity and peace. Later, competing minds, art, learning, and systems of government failed to settle it and produced confusion.

l: primeval man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity, with the Positive and Negative principles united and the seasons in order. He had knowledge but no occasion to use it, and all things and conditions were one.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Man's original integrity was scattered by systems of government, moral reform, goodness, intellectualism, art, and learning. He became unable to return to his natural instincts and original condition.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Sages may have lived outside mountains and forests, but their Virtue would still have remained hidden because the age was unsuitable. They preserved themselves by not exhausting the empire or Virtue with knowledge and by reverting to natural instincts.

l: retired scholars, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Retired scholars did not hide their bodies, words, or wisdom; their age was simply unsuitable for their mission. When their mission succeeded, they effaced themselves in prevailing unity, and when it failed, they relied on their own resources and waited.

l: Wisdom, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Knowledge was begotten out of repose and was not initially applied to any purpose. Later, knowledge was ornamented with rhetoric and used in ways that exhausted the empire, while learning overwhelmed the mind.

l: repose, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Repose is the condition through which the ancients cultivated TAO and begat knowledge. Knowledge and repose mutually produced each other, developing harmony and order.

l: government, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Government was introduced as Virtue declined, alongside systems of moral reform. Its development contributed to the loss of natural adaptation and original integrity.

l: natural instincts, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Natural instinct characterized man's original condition and the earlier unity of existence. Intellectualism, art, and learning caused man to lose it and prevented his return to it.

l: office, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Office was not originally considered attainment of desire because it was external and not part of oneself. In later times, office became identified with attainment of desire, although it could bring unhappiness.

l: happiness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Complete happiness means that nothing can be added to one's happiness and that one remains equally happy under all conditions. In the present age, both having and not having office cause unhappiness, so even happiness is not exempt from sorrow.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: During autumn floods, the Spirit of the River reaches the ocean and learns from the Spirit of the Ocean that his former sense of greatness was limited. The Spirit of the Ocean explains that space and time are without limits, dimensions and values are relative, and TAO is the unconditioned principle in which all things are equal. The dialogue contrasts the natural and the artificial and teaches that virtue consists in following the natural without sacrificing it to will or fame. The unit concerns the Spirit of the River, the Spirit of the Ocean, TAO, and the changing relations among all things.

l: Spirit of the River, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Spirit of the River rejoices when autumn floods swell the river and believes that all the beauty of the earth has gathered to him. After reaching the ocean, he recognizes his own insignificance and learns that greatness and smallness, value and worthlessness, and other distinctions are relative.

l: Spirit of the Ocean, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Spirit of the Ocean teaches the Spirit of the River about the limits of individual knowledge, the endlessness of time and space, and the relativity of dimensions and values. He explains TAO, the natural and artificial, and the need to let all things take their course.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: TAO is the only absolute and is without beginning or end. From the point of view of TAO, value and worthlessness, greatness and smallness, and other opposites have no fixed extremes, and all things are embraced without distinction.

l: river, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: During the autumn floods, every stream pours into the river, which swells in its turbid course until its banks are too far apart to distinguish a cow from a horse. The river is presented as small in relation to the ocean.

l: ocean, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The ocean receives all streams without overflowing and is constantly drained without becoming empty. It is described as immeasurably superior to rivers and brooks, yet still insignificant in comparison with the universe.

l: autumn floods, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The autumn floods cause every stream to pour into the river and make the river swell greatly. They begin the Spirit of the River's journey toward recognition of his own limitations.

l: man of TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The man of TAO has no reputation, and perfect virtue acquires nothing. Those who understand TAO do not suffer injury from without because they let all things take their course.

l: truly virtuous man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The truly great man does not injure others, seek gain, struggle for wealth, or ask help from others, but he takes no credit for these traits. He does not regard worldly ranks, emoluments, punishments, or shame as causes for joy or disgrace.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The man of perfect virtue cannot be harmed by fire, water, frost, sun, birds, or beasts because he discriminates between safety and danger. He remains happy in prosperous and adverse circumstances and is cautious about what he accepts and discards.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The universe gives the ocean its shape and is so vast that the ocean is like a small stone or tree on a mountain within it. The universe is also used to illustrate that opposing principles and conditions are mutually related.

l: the natural, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The natural abides within and virtue abides in the natural. Horses and oxen having four feet exemplifies the natural, which should not be obliterated by the artificial, will, or fame.

l: artificial, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The artificial is represented by putting a halter on a horse's head or a string through a bullock's nose. It abides without and must not be allowed to obliterate the natural.

l: greatness and smallness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Greatness and smallness are relative and cannot be defined as fixed extremes. The wise person does not regard the small as too little or the great as too much because dimensions have no limit.

l: Time, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Time is endless and cannot be arrested. Past years cannot be recalled, and every end is followed by a new beginning.

l: great Space, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Space is infinite, with no limit to movement in any direction. The wise person looks into space without treating the small as too little or the great as too much.

l: dimensions, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Dimensions are limitless, and terms describing them are not final. Both small and great things possess form, but no thing can be called absolutely the greatest or smallest.

l: value and worthlessness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Value and worthlessness have no absolute extremes from the point of view of TAO. Their determination depends on perspective, conditions, opportunity, and the impartial embrace of all creation.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Virtue abides in the natural and develops from knowledge of the natural and the artificial. It should not be sacrificed to fame, and perfect virtue is associated with freedom from injury by external circumstances.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The walrus, centipede, snake, wind, eye, and mind illustrate how each being has different natural qualifications, while the wind says that excelling in great things belongs only to the Sages. Confucius remains cheerful when surrounded because he regards failure as fate, success as opportunity, and danger without fear. Kung Sun Lung seeks Mou of Wei’s explanation of Chuang Tzŭ’s grandeur, but is compared to a frog confined to an old well and leaves humbled. Chuang Tzŭ rejects office, rebukes Hui Tzŭ’s suspicion, and argues with Hui Tzŭ about whether he can know the pleasure of minnows from the bridge over the Hao.

l: walrus, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The walrus envies the centipede’s many legs and nimble gait. It says that it hops about on one leg, unsuccessfully, and asks how the centipede manages its legs.

l: centipede, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The centipede explains that it does not consciously manage its legs; its mechanism works naturally. It tells the snake that despite having many legs, it cannot move as fast as the snake, whose natural mechanism requires no legs.

l: snake, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The snake is envied by the centipede because it moves quickly without legs. It tells the wind that although the snake has a form and can wriggle, the wind seems to be without form.

l: wind, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The wind says that anyone who can point at or kick it excels it, but that it can break huge trees and destroy large buildings. It explains that excelling in great things belongs only to the Sages.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The Sages are associated with excelling in great things rather than in every small thing.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: When Confucius visited K’uang, men of Wei surrounded him because they mistook him for Yang Hu. He continued playing and singing, explaining that failure is fate, success is opportunity, and the Sage remains fearless in great danger; the troops later apologized and withdrew.

l: failure, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Failure is described by Confucius as something determined by fate. In the days of Yao and Shun, no one throughout the empire was a failure, though no one recognized the gain.

l: success, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Success is described by Confucius as depending on opportunity. In the days of Chieh and Chou, no one throughout the empire was a success, though no one recognized the loss.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Fate is said by Confucius to be against him after he struggled against failure in vain. He says that knowing failure is fate and success is opportunity gives the Sage courage in great danger.

l: Kung Sun Lung, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Kung Sun Lung tells Mou of Wei that he had mastered many doctrines and arguments, but became astonished and unable to speak after hearing Chuang Tzŭ. He is compared to the frog in the well and leaves with his jaw dropped and tongue fixed to his palate.

l: Mou of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Mou of Wei listens to Kung Sun Lung’s request to explain the secret of Chuang Tzŭ’s grandeur. He responds by describing the frog in the old well, the turtle of the eastern sea, and the limits of narrow knowledge.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: TAO is identified with the way of the ancient Sages. Chuang Tzŭ is said to begin with chaos and return to TAO, moving beyond ordinary distinctions and argument.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Chuang Tzŭ is portrayed as surpassing Kung Sun Lung in grandeur and moving beyond ordinary distinctions, arguments, and the four points. He rejects administrative office by choosing to wag his tail in the mud, answers Hui Tzŭ’s suspicion with the story of the phœnix and owl, and debates Hui Tzŭ about knowing the pleasure of fishes.

l: well-frog, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The frog lives happily in an old well and believes that its limited surroundings are unsurpassed. After hearing the turtle describe the vast eastern sea, it is astonished and unable to answer; it represents knowledge confined to a narrow domain.

l: turtle of the eastern sea, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The turtle of the eastern sea cannot enter the well because its legs become stuck, so it retreats and describes the eastern sea’s vastness. It explains that the sea is not altered by long periods of flood or drought.

l: eastern ocean, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The eastern sea is described as too broad to measure with a thousand li and too deep to measure with a thousand fathoms. Its volume is not noticeably increased by years of flood or reduced by years of drought.

l: sacred tortoise, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The sacred tortoise of Ch’u has been dead for about three thousand years, and the prince keeps its remains enclosed in a chest on the ancestral altar. Chuang Tzŭ uses it to argue that being alive and wagging one’s tail in the mud is preferable to posthumous veneration.

l: Hui Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: Hui Tzŭ is prime minister in the Liang State and fears that Chuang Tzŭ wants his position, so he searches the state for three days and three nights. Chuang Tzŭ later tells him that his suspicion resembles an owl screeching at a passing phœnix, and Hui Tzŭ debates him over whether he can know the pleasure of fishes.

l: phœnix, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The phœnix flies from the southern sea to the northern sea, alighting only on the wu-t’ung tree and eating only bamboo fruit while drinking pure spring water. An owl with a rotten rat carcass screeches at it as it passes.

l: bridge over the Hao, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The bridge over the Hao is where Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ stroll when Chuang Tzŭ remarks on the pleasure of the minnows. Chuang Tzŭ says that he knows this pleasure from his own feelings on the bridge.

l: minnows, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The minnows are seen darting about beneath the bridge over the Hao. Chuang Tzŭ calls their movement pleasurable, while Hui Tzŭ questions how he can know their pleasure without being a fish.

l: fishes, Chuang Tzŭ, The walrus envies the centipede;
s: The fishes become the subject of the debate between Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ. Hui Tzŭ argues that Chuang Tzŭ cannot know their pleasure because he is not a fish, while Chuang Tzŭ says he infers it from his own feelings on the bridge.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The chapter asks whether perfect happiness exists and argues that the world’s pursuit of wealth, rank, comfort, and reputation does not secure it. It identifies inaction as true pleasure and connects it with the workings of Heaven and Earth, from which all changes arise. Chuang Tzŭ explains his acceptance of his wife’s death as a natural transformation, while stories of a hunchback, a skull, Confucius, and Lieh Tzŭ illustrate changing views of life, death, and happiness. The chapter also presents destiny as a pre-arrangement that limits what beings can become.

l: perfect happiness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Perfect happiness is said to consist in the absence of happiness and to be found only in inaction. The skull claims that death provides a happiness greater than that of a king.

l: TAO of inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Inaction is presented as true pleasure and as the only path to perfect happiness and preservation of life. Heaven and Earth do nothing, yet their inaction produces all the modifications of things.

l: happiness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Human happiness is questioned because ordinary people seem to find it in slavishly following the majority. The text says it is uncertain whether this common happiness is real.

l: physical well-being, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Physical well-being is used to judge the world’s pursuits of wealth, rank, old age, goodness, comfort, rich food, fine clothes, beauty, and music. The text says people can generally live well without these extras.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Life is described as a loan in which the borrower adds more dust and dirt to existence. It is presented as one phase in a sequence of transformations and as something that returns to the great Scheme.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Death is compared with night and with the natural transformations of the seasons. It is described as free from the sovereigns, subjects, and troubles of mortal life.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Destiny is described as a pre-arrangement that limits beings just as form has limitations. Confucius fears that Yen Yüan may fail to understand these limits when advising the prince of Ch'i.

l: the world, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The world esteems wealth, rank, old age, and goodness of heart, and enjoys comfort, rich food, fine clothes, beauty, and music. It regards inaction as great pain and treats people and creatures according to its own standards.

l: Heaven, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Heaven does nothing, yet it is clear. Its inaction contributes to all the modifications of things.

l: Earth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Earth does nothing, yet it enjoys repose. Its inaction, together with Heaven’s, produces the endless varieties of things.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Chuang Tzŭ accepts his wife’s death as a natural change from one phase to another and therefore refrains from weeping and wailing. He also questions a skull about the causes of its death and later hears it describe the happiness of death.

l: Yen Yüan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Yen Yüan goes east to the Ch'i State. Confucius worries that he may preach the Tao of Yao and Shun to the prince and thereby place himself in danger.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Confucius is sad when Yen Yüan travels to the Ch'i State. He teaches that destiny and form impose limits and warns that failing to understand a ruler’s nature can be fatal.

l: Lieh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Lieh Tzŭ sees an old skull while eating by the roadside and speaks to it about the uncertainty of life and death. He describes transformations among plants, insects, animals, and man as part of the great Scheme.

l: the skull, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The skull appears to Chuang Tzŭ in a dream and says that death has none of the troubles of mortal life and offers happiness greater than that of a king. It rejects Chuang Tzŭ’s offer to restore its body and return it to mortal relationships.

l: birth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Birth is described as a stage following the addition of substance to spirit and the assumption of form. It is one phase in a sequence of natural transformations that continues into death and return to the great Scheme.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The unit explains that life depends on nourishing both the physical body and the inner principle of vitality, while true perfection comes through harmony with TAO and God. Kuan Yin teaches Lieh Tzŭ that the perfect man achieves invulnerability through absolute purity, unity, and freedom from artificiality. Stories involving Confucius, skilled artisans, boatmen, fighters, and sages illustrate concentration, adaptation, inner security, and the need to care for both internal and external aspects of life. The unit concludes that natural spontaneity and freedom from self-conscious striving bring one near perfection.

l: The Secret of Life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Secret of Life concerns the simultaneous care of the internal self and the physical body. It teaches that nourishing the body alone is insufficient, while true fitness requires both body and vitality to be perfect.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: TAO is associated with the natural level reached by renouncing worldly cares and with the proper nourishment of both the internal and external aspects of life. Those who become one with God are described as near to TAO.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: God is the source of the natural intelligence, virtue, and perfection sought by the Sage. The text says that one whose physical frame and vitality are perfect is one with God, and that the perfect man brings his nature into partnership with God.

l: soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The soul is described as coming from God and as the principle that quickens the body. United with the body, it constitutes life.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Life comes and goes beyond human control, so nourishing the physical frame cannot by itself preserve it. The text says that life is sustained through simultaneous care of the body and the inner vitality.

l: body, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The physical body requires proper nourishment and must not be abandoned, although its care alone cannot ensure the preservation of life. The text also says that a perfect physical frame, joined with pure vitality, makes one fit for translation.

l: vitality, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Vitality is the subtle, immaterial principle that unites with matter to produce life. It can be dissipated by anger, preserved through inner care, and brought to its original purity through concentration and harmony.

l: internal self, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The internal self requires constant care alongside the physical body. Shan Pao cared for his inner self but neglected his external man, while Chang I cared externally but neglected the internal self; both failed to care for the lagging part.

l: Lieh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Lieh Tzŭ asks Kuan Yin how the perfect man can pass through solid bodies, fire, and great heights without harm. He receives an explanation that such feats arise from absolute purity rather than cunning.

l: Kuan Yin, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Kuan Yin teaches Lieh Tzŭ that the perfect man becomes secure through unity, inner strength, harmonized virtue, and partnership with God. He contrasts natural intelligence, which produces virtue, with artificial intelligence, which produces cunning.

l: perfect man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The perfect man can pass through solid bodies and fire without obstruction because he is in a condition of absolute purity. He is formless, beyond the reach of objective existences, and acts without dependence on self-confidence or authority.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Sage seeks refuge in God and is therefore free from harm caused by objective existences. The Sage also pursues natural intelligence and virtue rather than artificial cunning.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Confucius learns from a hunchback that singleness of purpose concentrates the faculties, and from a boatman’s account that skill requires freedom from attachment to external stakes. He also observes the cataract at Lü-liang, questions the old man who survives it, and concludes through several encounters that natural adaptation, concentration, and inner security are essential.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Chuang Tzŭ reflects on usefulness and uselessness through a huge tree and a goose, concluding that only alignment with TAO escapes the troubles of mortality. I Liao advises the prince of Lu to discard worldly power and human hindrances, while Pei Kung Shê explains that non-interference enabled the bells to be completed. Confucius undergoes the siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, learns about adaptation, God, and the dangers of fame, and is counseled by Tzŭ Sang Hu. Chuang Tzŭ also learns from a strange bird and from Yang Tzŭ that self-conscious virtue, pursuit of gain, and forgetfulness of one's nature lead to trouble.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Chuang Tzŭ says that a huge tree survives by being good for nothing, but later rests halfway between usefulness and uselessness. He is advised to roam with TAO, reflects on mortality and the human element, and learns from a strange bird that creatures injure one another through the pursuit of gain. He later concludes that he lost sight of his real self and withdraws from the world.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: TAO is presented as the domain containing a fixed point beyond the opposing conditions of worldly life. It enables one to move above mortality, remain without special effort, and harmonize with surroundings. Its expression through TÊ is concealed, purposeless, and unconcerned with merit or fame.

l: huge tree, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The huge tree is left standing because it is considered useless. Chuang Tzŭ says that its uselessness allows it to complete its allotted span.

l: goose, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The goose that does not cackle is selected for slaughter because it is useless. Its fate creates the dilemma between the usefulness and uselessness of the huge tree.

l: Life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Mortality brings troubles that cannot be avoided by merely appearing to be something one is not. Chuang Tzŭ says that being carried upon TAO and floating above mortality would remove such troubles.

l: human element, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The human element is described as a hindrance within oneself and a source of sorrow in others. I Liao says that the great Yao lacked this element and advises the prince of Lu to put off the hindrance and roam with TAO.

l: I Liao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: I Liao, identified as a sage of the Ch'u State, advises the prince of Lu that worldly efforts cannot secure freedom from misfortune. He urges the prince to discard power, lessen desires, and trust in TAO.

l: the prince of Lu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The prince of Lu is melancholy because, despite studying ancient doctrines and honoring religion and goodness, he cannot avoid misfortune. I Liao advises him to abandon worldly power, lessen desires, and travel inwardly toward TAO.

l: empty boat, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: An empty boat colliding with another boat does not provoke anger, even from an irritable person. The example shows that a person who could roam empty through life would be difficult to injure.

l: Pei Kung Shê, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Pei Kung Shê levies contributions to make bells and completes the work in three months. He explains that he showed no resentment or gratitude and allowed everyone to contribute what they wished, so no injury was done.

l: bells, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The bells, upper and lower, are all hung after three months of contributions. Their completion is attributed to Pei Kung Shê's non-interference and lack of resentment or gratitude.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Confucius is trapped between Ch'ên and Ts'ai and passes seven days without food. He learns from Jen and Tzŭ Sang Hu about avoiding fame, adapting to surroundings, friendship, God, and the limits of human knowledge. He later abandons his studies, returns home, and deepens his love for his disciples.

l: Tzŭ Sang Hu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Tzŭ Sang Hu tells Confucius that what is from God is valued above money and that the friendship of the superior man is negative like water. On another occasion, he recounts Shun's instructions concerning the physical body, feelings, and outward embellishment.

l: Yen Yüan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Yen Hui listens while Confucius explains that injury from God is easy to escape but the benefits of man are difficult to avoid. He asks about adaptation, beginnings and ends, and the unity of man and God.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: God is associated with the natural laws governing hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, which Confucius accepts as part of his allotted course. Confucius says that man is from God, that God is from God, and that death reunites man with God.

l: Tiao-ling, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Tiao-ling is the park where Chuang Tzŭ sees a strange bird in a chestnut grove. After the encounter, Chuang Tzŭ avoids leaving his house for three months.

l: strange bird, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The strange bird flies close to Chuang Tzŭ and lands in a chestnut grove, apparently forgetting its nature while pursuing prey. It first targets the mantis and cicada indirectly, then becomes prey itself because it forgets its own nature.

l: Yang Chu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Yang Tzŭ observes that the innkeeper loves the ugly concubine and dislikes the beautiful one because each is conscious of her appearance. He teaches that virtue should be practiced without conscious awareness of being virtuous.

l: adaptation, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Adaptation to surroundings is described as bringing rank and power, though such advantages are external and not derived from oneself. The swallow illustrates adaptation by avoiding unsuitable places and dwelling among men where it finds its natural abode.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Destiny is illustrated through the chain in which the cicada forgets itself, the mantis seizes the cicada, the strange bird seizes the mantis, and Chuang Tzŭ threatens the bird. The episode shows that loss follows the pursuit of gain.

l: the dilemma of usefulness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: The dilemma contrasts the huge tree, which survives because it is useless, with the goose, which dies because it is useless. Chuang Tzŭ rests halfway between usefulness and uselessness, but says that only TAO provides a fixed point beyond the dilemma.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: Death is described as the end that the Sage quietly awaits and as the point at which man is reunited with God. In the district called Established-Virtue, life is for enjoyment and death is for burial.

l: siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XX.
s: During the siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Confucius goes seven days without food. The experience leads to discussions of fear of death, adaptation, God, and the dangers of displaying knowledge and seeking fame.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The unit presents TAO as beyond words, formal morality, worldly distinctions, and deliberate cultivation, and as the source of inner freedom, happiness, and security amid change and death. T'ien Tzŭ Fang praises his tutor Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ to Prince Wên of Wei, while Confucius, Lao Tzŭ, and others illustrate how TAO is recognized through conduct rather than speech. Episodes involving Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, Duke Ai of Lu, Wên Wang, Lieh Yü K'ou, Sun Shu Ao, and the Princes of Ch'u and Fan show the effects of TAO or its absence on scholarship, government, courage, office, rank, and political survival.

l: T'ien Tzŭ Fang, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: T'ien Tzŭ Fang attends upon Prince Wên of Wei and praises Ch'i Kung for discoursing admirably upon TAO. He identifies Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ as his tutor and describes him as perfect, unconditioned, pure, and able to call people without TAO to a sense of error.

l: Prince Wên of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Prince Wên of Wei learns from T'ien Tzŭ Fang about Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ and becomes absorbed in silence. He concludes that his previous learning and the kingdom of Wei are sources of limitation and harm.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: TAO cannot be reached by superficial workers or by those who value worldly distinctions, and it is not adequately conveyed through speech or formal morality. It enables people to remain unmoved by change, rank, gain, loss, life, and death, and is associated with perfect goodness, happiness, and inner freedom.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The man of perfect virtue is described as outwardly human but inwardly divine, unconditioned yet able to engage with conditioned things, and pure yet tolerant of others. His virtue arises naturally rather than through deliberate cultivation.

l: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ initially refuses to meet a man of Lu because he considers the people of the Middle Kingdom skilled in ceremonies but lacking knowledge of the human heart. After meeting him twice, he sighs because the man behaves according to rigid forms while criticizing and admonishing him like a son and father.

l: Lu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Lu is where Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ twice encounters the same stranger and where Duke Ai later tests the distinction between scholars and people merely wearing scholars' robes.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Confucius remains silent when he meets Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ because, with such men, a look is enough for TAO to abide. He later explains that the perfect sages were unmoved by danger, seduction, rank, power, life, and death.

l: Yen Yüan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Yen Yüan says that he can imitate Confucius's walking, speaking, arguing, and preaching but cannot follow him beyond mortality. He is told that the death of the mind is the deepest sorrow, and later hears Confucius acknowledge the vastness of the universe after speaking with Lao Tzŭ.

l: Life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Human life is presented as a process of coming from somewhere and returning through death, with beginning and end following one another without a known exhaustion. Mortality should not destroy the peace of one who recognizes the unity of all things.

l: mind, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The mind is described as what informs the body, rises with life, and sets at death. Its death is more grievous than bodily death, although something that does not pass away remains amid the changing self.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Lao Tzŭ tells Confucius that he was wandering in the unborn and explains the interaction of passive Heaven and active Earth as producing harmony and all things. He teaches that perfect goodness and happiness come from recognizing the unity of creation and that the virtue of the perfect man is natural rather than cultivated.

l: First Cause, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The First Cause is suggested as the unseen source whose report fills space and whose work may account for darkness, light, recurring days and months, life, death, and the continual production of things. Its form is never witnessed.

l: Duke Ai of Lu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Duke Ai of Lu claims that Lu has many scholars because many people wear scholars' robes. After Chuang Tzŭ challenges this claim, he orders that death be the punishment for wearing the robes without TAO, and only one old man continues to wear them and withstands his questions.

l: scholars, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Scholars who wear round hats are said to know the seasons of Heaven, those with square shoes know the shape of Earth, and those with loose girdles are ready to decide questions. The text distinguishes genuine scholars who have TAO from people who merely wear scholars' robes.

l: Wên Wang, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Wên Wang seeks to employ the old man of Tsang in government and uses a supposed dream to satisfy his ministers and the vulgar mind. After the old man's administration succeeds, Wên Wang appoints him Grand Tutor and asks whether the government can extend over the empire.

l: old man of Tsang, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The old man of Tsang administers government without altering existing statutes or issuing unjust regulations. After three years, dangerous organisations are broken up, officials perform their duties naturally, and public and official interests become unified; he then refuses to answer Wên Wang's question and disappears.

l: Lieh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Lieh Yü K'ou demonstrates skilled archery under ordinary conditions by shooting while balancing a cup of water on his elbow. He becomes terrified on a precipice, and Po Hun Wu Jên concludes that his internal economy is defective and that he lacks TAO.

l: Po Hun Wu Jên, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Po Hun Wu Jên challenges Lieh Yü K'ou to shoot under extraordinary conditions and stands near the edge of a thousand-foot precipice without fear. He says that the perfect man can pass through extreme situations without changing countenance.

l: Sun Shu Ao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Sun Shu Ao remains emotionally steady after being appointed and dismissed from office three times. He regards gaining and losing office as outside his own self and says that concern with rank leaves no leisure for troubling over it.

l: rank and power, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Rank and power are treated as worldly conditions that do not affect a person who has TAO. The perfect sages and Sun Shu Ao remain unmoved by obtaining or losing office, and honour is said to reside in the person rather than in a changing condition.

l: Prince of Ch'u, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Prince of Ch'u is told that the preservation of the Ch'u State will not preserve his existence because he is without TAO. From this perspective, the Ch'us have not begun to exist even while the Fans have not begun to be destroyed.

l: Prince of Fan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Prince of Fan says that the destruction of the Fan State did not injure his existence. His statement contrasts an existence protected by TAO with the Prince of Ch'u's dependence on the preservation of his state.

l: Fan State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The destruction of the Fan State is presented as insufficient to injure the existence of the Prince of Fan. The state is contrasted with the individual existence that TAO places beyond mundane influences.

l: Ch'u State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The preservation of the Ch'u State is presented as insufficient to preserve the existence of the Prince of Ch'u. Its continued political existence is contrasted with the deeper existence associated with TAO.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Knowledge asks Do-nothing Say-nothing, All-in-extremes, and the Yellow Emperor how TAO may be known, approached, and attained; the Yellow Emperor teaches that it is found through no thoughts, no following, and no pursuit, while knowledge itself is treated as a barrier. The unit presents TAO as omnipresent, formless, nameless, spontaneous, and beyond speech, while all things contain it and arise, change, and return through it. It describes the universe and creation as beautiful, ordered, and governed by principles that human intellect cannot fully reach. Through teachings attributed to the Yellow Emperor, Chuang Tzŭ, Lao Tzŭ, Confucius, and others, the unit contrasts external adaptation and activity with internal constancy and passivity.

l: Knowledge, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Knowledge asks how TAO may be known, approached, and attained. He receives no answer from Do-nothing Say-nothing, hears that All-in-extremes has forgotten his answer, and is told by the Yellow Emperor that knowledge makes both of them wholly wrong.

l: Do-nothing Say-nothing, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Do-nothing Say-nothing cannot answer Knowledge's questions about TAO. The Yellow Emperor later calls him genuinely right because he does not know.

l: All-in-extremes, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: All-in-extremes begins to answer Knowledge's questions but forgets what he wants to say. He is described as near the truth because he has forgotten, and later considers the Yellow Emperor's words well spoken.

l: Yellow Emperor, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Yellow Emperor teaches that TAO is approached and attained through no thoughts, no resting, no following, and no pursuit. He says that those who understand TAO do not speak about it, and that knowledge of it makes Knowledge and himself wholly wrong.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: TAO cannot be brought, reached, heard, seen, spoken, or given a name, and it is not attained through knowledge. It is omnipresent and exists in all things, while causing fullness and emptiness, renewal and decay, beginning and ending, accumulation and dispersion without being any of them. Its operation is spontaneous, and the unit associates attainment of it with inaction, silence, and non-discussion.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Virtue is described as the exemplification of TAO. It cannot be reached directly, though it may beautify a person and is contrasted with charity, duty to one's neighbour, and ceremonies.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Sage teaches a doctrine that does not find expression in words. The true Sage performs nothing beyond gazing at the universe, adapts to external circumstances without violating or clinging to relationships, and finds salvation in addition without gain and diminution without loss.

l: universe, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The universe is described as very beautiful and silent, with its four seasons following fixed laws. Its countless evolutions, deaths, births, forms, and transformations cannot be fully grasped by human intellect.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: God is presented as the source of delegated body, life, individuality, and posterity. The unit says that bodily movement, rest, taste, and the operations of life follow God's laws.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Creation is based on absolute principles but does not speak. It is continually informed by TAO, and its apparent destruction leaves immaterial existence; its order is governed by the Yin, the Yang, and the four seasons.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Confucius discusses perfect TAO with Lao Tzŭ and teaches Jen Ch'iu that before the universe existed there was TAO. He also teaches Yen Yüan that people should modify themselves externally while remaining internally constant, and that the best language is unspoken and the best action is without deeds.

l: vital fluid, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Vital fluid is said to produce life through its convergence and death through its dispersion. Life is described as a concentration of vital fluid, with its duration varying by an inappreciable amount.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Kêng Sang Ch'u, a disciple of Lao Tzŭ, benefits the people of Wei-lei but rejects their attempt to exalt him, fearing that this departs from TAO. Nan Yung Ch'u seeks guidance first from Kêng Sang Ch'u and then from Lao Tzŭ, who teaches him to preserve life by maintaining inner unity, repose, and freedom from disturbances. Lao Tzŭ describes TAO as the source of TÊ, life, Nature, and all divisions, while Non-Existence and existence are ultimately one. The unit also examines the subjective point of view, the obstacles to TAO, and the spontaneity required for virtue and action.

l: Kêng Sang Ch'u, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Kêng Sang Ch'u, who alone among Lao Tzŭ's disciples had attained TAO, benefited the district of Wei-lei by dismissing the systematically clever and conventionally charitable. When the people wished to honour him as a Sage or tutelary god, he felt ashamed, believing this showed that he had departed from Lao Tzŭ's doctrine. He later told Nan Yung Ch'u to preserve his form, secure his vitality, and avoid anxious thoughts, but directed him to Lao Tzŭ for further instruction.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Lao Tzŭ questioned Nan Yung Ch'u before hearing his intended questions and recognized his confusion. He taught Nan Yung Ch'u that preserving life requires keeping all in ONE, knowing when to stop, attending to oneself, and remaining without care and excessive knowledge. He further explained the conditions of the perfect man, the nature of TAO, and the need to reject disturbances and artificiality.

l: Nan Yung Ch'u, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Nan Yung Ch'u asked how he could attain TAO while avoiding the harms caused by ignorance, knowledge, lack of charity, charity, and duty to his neighbour. After receiving limited instruction from Kêng Sang Ch'u, he travelled to Lao Tzŭ, described his confusion, and sought the art of preserving life. He attempted self-cultivation but remained troubled until Lao Tzŭ continued his instruction.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: TAO operates without a visible agent, remains the same through different spheres of action, and can be divided without ceasing to be entire. It is infinite as Space and Time, unconditioned, and the source from which existence and all subdivisions proceed. TAO is the sovereign lord of TÊ, and following it requires spontaneity, inaction, and freedom from the twenty-four disturbances and obstructions.

l: perfect man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The perfect man may be hidden like a corpse in a tomb while people become unartificial and without care. He shares the food of the earth but the happiness of God, avoids trouble from men and things, and acts without joining in censure, plotting, or toadying. He can devote himself profitably to the natural and artificial alike and is capable of entering the eternal harmony of God.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Sage abides where the tenuity of mortality shares the formless. He devotes himself to the natural and neglects the artificial, and his knowledge stops at the unknowable. His practice may bring no reputation, yet it throws a halo around the meanest.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: God assists those who are constant and makes them his chosen children. God punishes those who do evil in secret, and calamities that come despite proper self-cultivation are attributed to God rather than man. The perfect man seeks harmony with God and is not disturbed by praise or insult.

l: Nature, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Nature is described as the substance of life and as a powerful bandit from which there is no escape. Its interaction with the Positive and Negative principles produces the visible universe. Nature itself does not injure; man's own heart causes the injury.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: TÊ is the virtue of spontaneity and is glorified through life. TAO is its sovereign lord, while life manifests it. Emotion that is spontaneous is called virtue passive, and emotion not evoked by the external is called virtue active.

l: Nothing, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Non-Existence is described as the Portal of God and as the source from which all things sprang. Existence could not make existence exist, and Non-Existence and Nothing are one. The Sage's abiding-place is connected with this formless state.

l: Portal of God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Portal of God is the passage through which one enters and leaves without seeing its form. It is identified with Non-Existence, from which all things arise.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Virtue is entangled by hate, ambition, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, and it is obstructed by rejecting, adopting, receiving, giving, knowledge, and ability. When these influences are not allowed to run riot, the mind becomes ordered, reposeful, clear, unconditioned, and capable of inaction. Virtue is also associated with spontaneous emotion arising from the real self.

l: spontaneity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Spontaneity is essential to TAO and is expressed through natural, unforced emotion and action. Perfect politeness, duty, wisdom, charity, and trust are described as spontaneous rather than artificial or calculated. The Sage follows necessity, which is the TAO of the Sage.

l: art of preserving life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The art of preserving life consists in keeping all in ONE, losing nothing, knowing when to stop and how much is enough, leaving others alone, attending to oneself, and remaining without cares and excessive knowledge. It is illustrated by the child, whose constitutional harmony allows it to act, move, and adapt without conscious calculation. Lao Tzŭ later connects it with freedom from trouble, repose, and unconscious adaptation to circumstances.

l: subjective point of view, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The subjective point of view begins with life and, guided by knowledge, develops into judgments of right and wrong. People mistake their own standards for universal standards and value usefulness, success, and present circumstances according to limited perspectives. The text presents every part of a thing as capable of being a point of view and treats individual standards as fallible.

l: existence, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Existence has no limitation and is paired with continuity without a starting-point, which is Time. Birth is not a beginning and death is not an end, while existence and Non-Existence are ultimately one. The text presents life and death as stages within a larger unity.

l: Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Man's will is called the most deadly weapon, and man's heart rather than Nature is said to cause injury. Man becomes confused by artificial distinctions, emotional disturbances, ambition, and the desire for reputation or pre-eminence. He can approach TAO by cultivating repose, adapting to necessity, and freeing himself from artificiality.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Hsü Wu Kuei visits Wu Hou of Wei and argues that passion, moral schemes, love for the people, and duty towards one's neighbour obstruct natural virtue and lead to disorder and war. He teaches that rulers should abstain from aggression and govern like the boy cares for horses, allowing natural conditions to remain unharmed. The Yellow Emperor meets the boy, who directs him toward TAO and teaches that government requires no more than preventing harm. Chuang Tzŭ disputes Hui Tzŭ and the competing schools over moral standards, then mourns the loss of Hui Tzŭ as a worthy interlocutor.

l: Hsü Wu Kuei, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Hsü Wu Kuei visits Wu Hou of Wei and tells him that passion, loves, and hates harm his natural condition and senses. He argues against love for the people and duty towards one's neighbour as artificial causes of disorder, urging inward sincerity and non-aggression instead. He later teaches the Prince that nourishment and spiritual health concern rulers and common people alike.

l: Wu Hou of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Wu Hou of Wei receives Hsü Wu Kuei and is told that his sensual rule oppresses his population while harming his soul. He wishes to love his people and end war through duty towards one's neighbour, but Hsü Wu Kuei says this approach will be disastrous.

l: Nü Shang, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Nü Shang introduces Hsü Wu Kuei to Wu Hou of Wei and later questions him about the words that pleased the Prince. Hsü Wu Kuei explains that the Prince was moved by hearing about dogs and horses and by encountering the voice of a pure man.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: TAO is presented as something that cannot be reached through fixed moral schemes, cleverness, or demonstrations of unusual powers. The boy knows where TAO abides, and Lu Chü's account of tuned lutes illustrates TAO as harmony rather than mere technical effect.

l: TÊ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Natural virtue is obstructed when a ruler gives free play to passion or imposes artificial moral standards. Hsü Wu Kuei advises cultivating the sincerity within one's breast so it responds to circumstances without aggression.
